reviews.review:
Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

Edit 2016: what I've said before still applies. I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382 

****DISCLAIMER:****
 WIll not actually refund any purchases if you are somehow not pleased with the overall game. 
Mouse and Mechanical Keyboard sold seperatly.
Batteries not included.

Well, I should probably say that I didn't necessarily expect one of my new favorite games of all time to be an overglorified super-hacker OS simulator, but here I am now, I guess. 

There's so much detail put into this game and it ends up becoming extremely challenging. There's a lot of learning to do in terms of what programs you need to utilize in different situations and generally how to use the interface (especially if you're not too amazingly tech-savvy). I, myself, don't consider myself anywhere near a technological expert, but I was still very easily able to get the hang of it largely due to the intricate way the game was structured and paced. There were so many things that were beautiful about this game, and I admittedly got addicted to this game. It'll probably be a game that I'll often pick back up and play over and over again in the future, and I certainly don't have any complaints in that regard. 

It may be off limits to people who are easily confused or who tend to give up on things quickly once they become overwhelmed with new information, but otherwise, this game is easily worth over $40. It's $10. Just get it.

This is a great hacking game that uses command prompts in order to do things. The game begins with you receiving an email via a Dead Man Switch, which is something that is sent if certain conditions are met(or not), such as not turning on your computer for a week. This email sent to you was from a Hacker named Bit. He didn't log on after 2 weeks, so the email was auto sent to you. It said that 'if you're reading this, I'm already dead'. The game continues into a tutorial where you complete the tasks that Bit set up to be sent to you as you finish them.

This is the premise of the story(no spoilers in that btw). You go through this hacking world trying to find out what happened to bit. You can explore the various computers you come across in your travels, read the various text documents that can contain story related content, whether it be main quest or side quest, or joke texts. There's a site called Bash.org in real life, and it archives funny quotes that people submit that the found on various IRC(chat rooms) conversations. Hacknet is filled with many text documents, usually starting with "IRC" then numbers. They're very funny, and you can even collect them if you wish.

Hacknet is a lot like Uplink, but more modern and polished. There's organizations that give you missions/side quests for you to do, and they're all interesting in some way. The side quests are required to a fair degree, as Bits messages wont tell you more until your skill improves by going up in rank on these Organizations. It's not just randomly generated quests like in Uplink, where the differences in quests was basically names and numbers. All of Hacknets Side Quests/Missions have little stories, and as you do these contracts, you may end up finding text documents that hint at what happened to Bit.

For the actual gameplay, it starts out simple, with a few programs to help break through security You'll find more programs to help you get into more complicated systems. 

Now for how Hacknet is different from Uplink. For one thing, there's no upgrades. You can find hacking programs, but there's no upgrading, no hacking store to buy hacking upgrades/software. There's no money actually, and no upgrading your computer. Instead of grinding money to get a more powerful PC and just bulldoze your way through security in Uplink, you need to use your programs and computer more strategically.

This DOSE lower replay value compared to Uplink. In Uplink there's plenty of things to buy and upgrade, and unlimited, if not plain, missions to do. Hacknet is more story driven, with it's main story and the little side stories filled with interesting jobs, info, chat logs, and lots of other things.

I'm not sure how far I am exactly, but at the very least, there's about 35+ side quests at the very least. So there's plenty to do in this game, along with Easter eggs and subtle references to entertain you.

While Uplink was more mouse driven in how you hack, Hacknet is almost entirely with keyboard commands, like Spencer's Hacker Evolution games(The first 2, not the shitty Duality). There is some mouse controls, such as using the mouse to quickly move through a computers directories.

If you like Uplink, you will definitely like Hacknet. If you're interested in hacking games, but haven't played one before, this COULD be a good start, as the difficulty curve is very fair, but Uplink might be better for a newbie.

Btw, you can use the TAB key to auto complete words/directories/programs names. Useful for when you need to quickly break through many ports.

Don't let the terminal screen and techno-nonsense trick you—Hacknet is a deceptively simple game to play. You use a series of commands to "hack" into terminals both as a contract hacker and on a mission, one to find the reason for a fellow hacker's untimely death.

It's in large part due to its phenomenal soundtrack and well-realised interface, but no game this year has made me feel like more of a badass than Hacknet. Its presentation is executed so well that every action you take feels like you've been doing them for years, like hacking into networks is just child's play.

It plays very much like a puzzle-adventure game, so if something like that is up your alley, it's really worth checking out.

Also, it's worth playing to see the final hacking sequence alone.

While the game itself is fun, the story progress (and thus, the whole savegame) can be destroyed too easily by deleting important files. For example, various contracts can only be fulfilled by answering specific mails, if you delete those, you cannot proceed (some mails state that you have to reply, but some don't even if you have to).

Besides being the best hacking simulator I've ever played, Hacknet is one of the best games I've played for a long time. Great gameplay and great story. Team Fractal Alligator did a great job and I'm eagerly waiting for their next project.

Welcome to typing simulator 2015. And I mean that in a completely good way. This game was truly excelent. A great puzzler that affords you all the tools you need, but doesn't hold your hand. Excellent story telling as well, both serious, and with a good bit of inside humor. 

As a reccomendation, for a good authentic feeling (as well as skill building) REALLY try to type console commands as much as possible, even for basic navigation and such. 

Looking forward to this teams next endeavor.

Hacknet is one of those games that when you start it up for the first time, you want to play all the way through. While It was only a few hours to beat, it was still quite the challenge of intelect and perception. Me beating it didn't stop me from playing through it again at least 7 times before inviting my friends to buy it as well. The game itself is unique and requires the "very difficult" skill of "typing without error". If you can type, you can play this game, and you WILL get better as time goes on. A story that thouroughly intrigued me with a satisfying ending. I truly believe it is 10$ worth spending for hours upon hours of fun.
Great game. But really, really short for $10.
